chapter_theme: Three songs at Thiruppukkoliyur (திருப்புக்கொளியூர், the old name of Avinasi): Murugan as the guru of the Siva-yogis, a praise that recalls Siva's acts for Sundarar, and the poet himself besieged by Kama's army at evening.

946.reading: The poet says he will not forget the wondrous feet of Murugan, the true guru who, to ripe Siva-yogis of disciplined conduct and silence who eat only greens and with devotion pass beyond the thirty-six tattvas to the supportless state of release, gave in that very moment the teaching of jnana, so that their deluding faults fell away. The praise names him the fierce hero with twelve arms, the lord of Vayalur where blue lilies and pearl-bright pools spread fragrance, the golden-bodied lord of Avinasi, who gives grace to truth so that the false Kali age departs, at Pukkoliyur.
946.nuance: ஆறாறு தத்துவ மேல் வீடு பற்று நிராதார நிலை: the thirty-six tattvas of Saiva doctrine are passed, and release is held as a state without support. The teaching acts instantly (அக்கணமே). The song asks nothing for the poet beyond not forgetting the feet.

947.reading: The first half pictures Indra's white elephant and Indra living in the shade of the kalpaka tree in his splendid city with the gods around him, and asks the Kumara of lordly form to appear and rule the poet, the life of Vayalur. The second half recalls Siva's acts for his devotee Sundarar: the thousand gold coins sought from shrine to shrine for the woman of Kamalalayam, the Lord coming as a Brahmin in the forest to untie a packet of rice for the tired singer, and at Avinasi the child called back from the crocodile's mouth; Murugan is the Lord whom that lord of Pukkoliyur praises.
947.nuance: The song is almost wholly praise and its hero is Sundarar (தொண்டர்), served by Siva as friend and helper (சகாயன்). செறிப்பித்த கராவதின் வாய் மக அழைப்பித்த is the boy swallowed by a crocodile at Avinasi and restored at Sundarar's song. The first half is hard to construe, and its link to the plea எனை ஆள் is uncertain.

948.reading: The poet pictures evening as a battle: Kama, called by the cuckoo, rides the chariot of the breeze with flower arrows and the moon as his hanging garland, the sea as his war drum, and draws his sugarcane bow; caught in the arts of fragrant-haired women he is dying, and asks whether this pleases the compassionate one and when he will reach the jnana that is the Name by which it is crossed. The praise names Murugan the lover of the millet-field girl, son of the lord with the crescent in his hair, the vel that took Sura's life, and nephew of the heroic Rama who dammed the sea and made Ravana's crowns fly, at the festival town of Pukkoliyur.
948.nuance: The akam convention of evening as the hour when love's pain grows, usually given to a woman, is here the poet's own, armed as Kama's march (படை கூடி மேலெழா அணி வகுத்து). கடக்கப்படு நாமமான ஞானம்: the knowledge that crosses it is a Name, presumably Murugan's.

links.note: Both make evening the hour when love's sickness is fullest: the Kural's woman says it buds in the morning and opens at evening; 948 gives that hour to the poet himself and arms it as Kama's army of breeze, moon, cuckoo and sea.
